title: Mixtures and separating
intro: Dissolving, filtering, evaporating, distilling and chromatography: learn how to get substances back out of a mixture.
description: Free KS3 Chemistry questions with answers on mixtures and separating techniques: dissolving, solutions, filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9.

questions.q: Salt is stirred into water and disappears. What has happened?
questions.hint: Melting needs heat. Here the salt spreads out in the water.
questions.explain: The salt dissolved: its particles spread out between the water particles. It's still there, which is why the water tastes salty.

questions.q: In salt water, what is the **solvent**?
questions.hint: The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving.
questions.explain: Water is the solvent, salt is the solute, and salt water is the solution.
Insoluble means it doesn't dissolve, like sand in water. Soluble means it does, like sugar.

questions.q: 10 g of salt is dissolved in 100 g of water. What is the mass of the salt water?
questions.explain: Mass is conserved when something dissolves: 100 + 10 = 110 g.

questions.q: A solution where no more solid will dissolve is called…
questions.explain: A saturated solution can't dissolve any more solute at that temperature. Warming it usually lets more dissolve.

questions.q: How can you separate sand from water?
questions.hint: Sand doesn't dissolve. What can catch the grains?
questions.explain: Filter paper lets water through but traps the sand, which is insoluble.

questions.q: How can you get salt back from salt water?
questions.hint: Salt is dissolved, so filtering won't catch it.
questions.explain: Heat the salt water so the water evaporates. The salt crystals are left behind.

questions.q: Which method separates the different coloured inks in a felt-tip pen?
questions.hint: You put a dot of ink on paper and let water soak up it.
questions.explain: In chromatography, the colours travel different distances up the paper, so they separate.

questions.q: How can you separate iron filings from sand?
questions.explain: Iron is magnetic and sand isn't, so a magnet pulls out the iron.

questions.q: How can you get pure drinking water from sea water?
questions.hint: Boil it, then cool the steam back into a liquid.
questions.explain: In distillation the water boils, the steam is cooled in a condenser and turns back into pure liquid water. The salt stays behind.

questions.q: A mixture contains sand, salt and water. What is the best order to separate all three?
options: Filter to remove the sand, then evaporate the water to get the salt
questions.hint: Which part can a filter catch?
questions.explain: Filtering removes the insoluble sand. The salty water goes through, and evaporating it leaves the salt.

questions.q: In chromatography, why do two inks travel different distances?
options: They dissolve in the solvent and stick to the paper by different amounts
One ink is heavier than the paper
The paper is wetter at the top
questions.hint: Think about how much each ink “likes” the water compared with the paper.
questions.explain: Each substance dissolves in the solvent and sticks to the paper by a different amount, so they move up at different speeds.

questions.hint: A science word can mean something different from everyday life.
questions.explain: In science a pure substance contains only one substance. Bottled water labelled “pure” is actually a mixture with minerals dissolved in it.

questions.q: How can you tell if a sample of water is pure?
options: It boils at exactly 100 °C (at normal air pressure)
questions.hint: Pure substances melt and boil at one fixed temperature.
questions.explain: Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal air pressure. Dissolved substances change the boiling point and make water boil over a range of temperatures.

questions.q: A solid melts slowly between 72 °C and 79 °C. What does this tell you?
options: It is probably a mixture, not pure
questions.hint: Pure substances melt at one sharp temperature.
questions.explain: A pure substance has a sharp melting point. Melting over a range suggests a mixture.

questions.q: Which of these is a mixture?
questions.hint: Which one has lots of different substances in it?
questions.explain: Orange juice contains water, sugars, acids and much more, so it's a mixture.
